A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SkyLadder and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite reorganization, renumbering, and additional material in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining experiments, downstream evaluations, scheduling ablations, attention analyses, and training-time measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds long-context evaluations, architecture comparisons, training-stability measurements, and dataset analyses.

M1.justification: The blockwise causal mask, linear window-expansion rule, integration with intra-document masking, and Flash Attention pseudocode retain the same procedure. Hybrid-attention and Qwen-style models are additional experimental configurations; no new SkyLadder algorithmic component is specified.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix A.7.3 substantially expands evaluation coverage with TOEFL and QuALITY reading comprehension, PopQA within retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot classification on DBpedia, AGNews, Amazon, Yelp, and SST2. Existing training corpora and earlier evaluation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Random, IntraDoc, BM25, Dataset Decomposition with one or eight cycles, continual pretraining, and alternative schedules. New architecture and task experiments compare Random with SkyLadder rather than introducing another competing algorithm. The expanded discussion of Li and Jin does not establish additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Gemma3-like 120M/360M and Qwen2.5-0.5B experimental configurations, stability measurements over the first 30K training steps, and FLOPs evaluation. Its new McNemar tests use full benchmark test sets, explicitly distinguished from OLMES's sampled evaluations. These are additions to the experimental design; the original training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's attention-sink and entropy analysis, v2 Section 4.6 investigates maximum attention logits, loss fluctuations, and gradient norms across context lengths. Appendix A.7.4 adds tests of applicability to hybrid attention and Qwen-style architectures, while A.10 analyzes corpus and benchmark length distributions. Existing scheduling ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates and a heuristic loss-difference threshold. v2 introduces paired McNemar significance tests for the main benchmark comparisons, with significance markers in Table 1 and procedures in A.7.3. Its checklist newly states that pretraining runs were not repeated because of cost; this is disclosure, not an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Most existing benchmark scores are retained, but Table 7 changes continual pretraining's long-context score from 2.7 to 10.0 under the same reported schedule. New results include Random versus SkyLadder RAG averages of 30.3 versus 35.5 and many-shot classification averages of 73.9 versus 76.5. v2 also adds architecture, stability, dataset-statistics, and FLOPs results, including reported compute reductions of 14.7% and 26.3%.

T1.justification: v2 A.6 adds an explicit mathematical definition of per-token context size as the number of accessible, unmasked tokens and derives its uniform distribution under Random causal masking. v1 displayed this distribution without that formalization. The scheduling mathematics is unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs of effectiveness.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central findings and contribution: shorter contexts improve standard-task learning, and short-to-long scheduling improves performance and efficiency while preserving long-context capability. The headline claims of gains up to 3.7% and training-time savings up to 22% remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an optimization-stability explanation connecting shorter contexts to smaller attention logits, smoother losses, and more controlled gradients. It newly attributes RULER differences to synthetic-benchmark variability and discusses compatibility with alternative attention architectures. Appendix A.1 explicitly identifies computational scaling limits and the absence of theoretical analysis; Section 4.3 also narrows improvement over IntraDoc from all benchmarks to many.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial resource and data documentation: A.9 specifies A100/H100 hardware and training costs, including approximately 200 hours on eight A100s for a 1B, 8K-context run; A.10 supplies corpus and benchmark length statistics; A.11 supplies asset licenses. It also clarifies baseline use of Flash Attention 2. The code link, core configuration tables, and implementation pseudocode already existed in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Gemma3, Kimi K2, and additional reading-comprehension benchmarks, and replaces the unrelated Zhang 2020 citation for SlimPajama with its actual dataset reference. Appendix A.8 expands comparisons with sequence-length warmup and GrowLength, while retaining the original positioning around simultaneous efficiency and performance gains.

P1.justification: The main five-section narrative remains recognizable. v2 tightens wording, moves coding experiments into the results subsection, and consolidates efficiency, attention analysis, and related-method comparison under Analysis and Discussion. It expands appendix organization and adds a conference checklist, but largely preserves the existing exposition rather than rewriting the paper wholesale.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-stability plot and tables for stability, new tasks, architectures, and dataset statistics. It moves long-context columns from Table 1 into Table 2, adds significance markers and a FLOPs column, and revises captions. The NeurIPS formatting also substantially changes typography, equation placement, and figure/table positioning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for preserving long-context capability: v1 relied mainly on MDQA/RULER, whereas v2 adds broader 3B reading-comprehension, retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot evaluations. Architecture tests and stability diagnostics address generality and mechanism, while significance testing and resource disclosures improve assessability. These gains address important validation gaps rather than merely increasing reported performance. Statistical assurance remains incomplete because training runs are not repeated and the McNemar significance threshold is unspecified.
